content.text:
I weighed the item against the scope note that van der Waals constants are out of scope as calculation inputs, and the item only reads them as a ranking of attraction strength, with no calculation. The stem asks "which gas deviates most," and the skill tag is 4.B, so I checked it against that.

The main problem is the skill fit. The task is a direct lookup of the largest a value, and nothing asks the student to judge a model against chemical theory. The stem also never says which gas deviates most "from the ideal gas model" because of what theory. A 4.B item would ask the student to evaluate a claim or explanation.

The key itself holds up. CO2 has the largest a, and it also has the largest b (about 0.0427 L/mol, versus 0.0318 for O2, 0.0428 for CH4 and 0.0322 for Ar). It is also the most easily liquefied of the four (critical temperature 304 K), so it deviates most at 20 atm and 300 K. Both effects point to CO2, so there is a unique answer.

The distractor explanations are all the same template, "smaller than 3.59 of CO2". They do not name distinct misconceptions such as thinking that smaller or lighter molecules deviate more, or that polarity is what matters. The options also give no giveaway beyond the table.

On exam suitability, the item is quick and has no arithmetic, but it is too trivial and is a pure table lookup.
